newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU sees single currency rivalling dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU sees single currency rivalling dollar.

text.p: A single European currency will gradually rival the dollar on global markets and become a major international currency, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

"The development of the euro into a major international currency will be gradual, but relatively important in those countries which have close links with the EMU-participating countries," the Commission said in a report.
Trade relations with countries immediately outside monetary union are likely to give the euro the role of an anchor currency.

"The countries of central and eastern Europe which already tie their currencies to the mark will be linked to the euro ipso facto," the study said, adding that such links could extend to Mediterranean and African countries.

Another factor in favour of the euro is the EU's relative weight in global trade. In 1996 the EU's share of gross domestic product in the OECD amounted to 38.3 percent, as against 32.5 percent for the United States and 20.5 percent for Japan.
Although a large percentage of world trade is currently priced in dollars, this could change once the euro is introduced.

In its first attempt to assess the international effects of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the Commission played down speculation that an excess of dollar reserves would be created once the single currency is launched.
"Speculation on possible effects arising from excess dollar reserves is not founded," the study said.
The creation of a European Central Bank (ECB) is widely expected to result in a rise in dollar reserves among central banks participating in the euro -- often dubbed the dollar overhang.
But economists are divided over just how large the dollar surplus would be.

The Commission noted that the EU currently holds more foreign exchange reserves than the United States or Japan and might be disproportionate to the bloc's needs after the single currency is launched.
Two reasons are given for this potential imbalance. First, with the elimination of national currencies there will less need to hold reserves for intervention purposes.
Secondly, trade flows inside the new monetary bloc will take place in euros, further diminishing the need for large dollar reserve holdings.

One of major worries of such an outcome is that the excess dollars might be sold on global currency markets, leading to a sharp fall in the U.S. currency's value. The Commission's study minimised the likelihood of such a scenario.
"Although the absolute value of the amounts involved may indeed be substantial, they are not significant in view of the turnover in financial markets," the study said.
Moreover, central banks will be fully aware of the potential impact on exchange rates of their transactions, therefore any attempts to reduce the dollar overhang will likely be gradual.
Regarding the potential for private portfolios to readjust as a result of the euro's introduction, the Commission said that it was very difficult at this stage to ascertain the likely effects.
"Traders within the euro area that previously kept different European currencies to diversify their risk may be faced with a surplus for euros for transaction purposes," the Commission added.
Alternatively, those who were not previously invested in European currencies might want to readjust their portfolios to include the euro.
